subject: 고대 도시의 상수도와 위생
title: Water and waste in the ancient city
content: Ancient cities were limited in size less by their food supply than by their water, and the engineering that solved this constraint is among the most durable evidence they left. Aqueducts carried water for many miles on a gradient that had to be maintained within a fraction of a degree, and the surveying required was substantial. Where such works were built, the population that a settlement could support rose sharply, and the archaeological record shows dense quarters appearing within a generation of their completion. What the same record shows less often is any comparable attention to waste. Drains existed, and some were impressive, but they were designed chiefly to carry rainwater off the streets rather than to remove sewage from houses. Refuse accumulated in courtyards and alleys, and the layers that archaeologists excavate are thick with it. Ancient writers who praised the aqueducts of their cities said little about what happened to the water once it had been used. This asymmetry is informative rather than merely disappointing. Bringing water in was a public work that a ruler could commission and inscribe his name upon, whereas removing waste required households to change what they did daily, and no inscription commemorates that. The health of an ancient city therefore improved much less than its water supply would suggest, and skeletal evidence from urban cemeteries of the period shows the cost. Cities grew because water arrived, and they remained unhealthy because the arrangements that would have made them clean were not the kind that anyone built monuments to.

subject: 수렵채집에서 정착으로 — 초기 농경 마을
title: The first villages and the long transition
content: The shift from foraging to farming is often described as a revolution, and the word suggests a decision taken once and then spread. Excavation of the earliest villages tells a slower story. At many sites people built permanent houses, ground wild grain, and stored it for centuries before any plant shows the changes that domestication produces. They were settled before they were farmers, and the sequence has to be explained rather than assumed away. What appears to have held them in place was abundance rather than scarcity. Certain regions offered dense stands of wild cereals, nuts, and game within a small radius, so a community could remain in one location through the year without exhausting it. Once settled, however, the community acquired properties that foraging groups had not needed. Storage had to be guarded, houses represented investment that could not be carried away, and the population grew because a settled mother could raise children spaced more closely than a mobile one could. Farming then followed as a response to conditions the settlement itself had created. The stored grain that people replanted was selected without anyone intending to select it, and the plants changed over generations. When climate turned against the wild stands, the villages that had already begun tending crops could continue, and those that had not were abandoned. What the record describes is therefore less a discovery than a trap that closed gradually behind people who had entered it for entirely different reasons.

subject: 고대 문명의 관개와 국가 형성
title: Irrigation and the ancient state
content: An old argument holds that irrigation created the ancient state. Canals of any size demand coordinated labour, and the authority that organizes digging and allocates water was said to harden into government. The hypothesis was attractive because it linked a visible engineering achievement to a political outcome, and it fitted the great river valleys where the earliest civilizations appeared. Excavation has since complicated the sequence in a way that deserves attention. The earliest canals at several ancient sites were small, and they served single communities that managed them without any central authority. Systems of that scale can be maintained by households that share the water and settle their disputes among themselves, and ethnographic study of surviving arrangements shows exactly this. Large works appear later, after states already existed, which reverses the direction the hypothesis proposed. What the state contributed was not the invention of irrigation but its extension beyond what neighbours could negotiate. A revised account gives water a role that is real but indirect. Irrigated land yields more reliably than rain-fed land, and reliable yields make surplus predictable enough to tax. An authority that could assess and store that surplus had a resource its neighbours lacked, and it used that resource to build the larger canals that then supported more people still. Irrigation did not create the ancient state so much as it gave an emerging one something worth collecting, and the monumental systems that survive belong to the end of the process rather than its beginning.

subject: 신석기 혁명은 건강에 어떤 영향을 주었나
title: What farming did to ancient health
content: The adoption of agriculture is usually presented as an improvement in the human condition, and in one respect it plainly was, since farming supported far more people on the same land. Skeletal evidence from the centuries on either side of the transition complicates the picture considerably. Compared with the foragers who preceded them, early farmers were shorter, showed more signs of arrested growth in childhood, and carried more dental disease. Their bones record episodes of illness and hunger that the earlier population had not experienced to the same degree. Several causes appear to have combined. A diet narrowed to a few cereals supplied calories but fewer of the nutrients a varied foraging diet had provided, and the starch it contained fed the bacteria that damage teeth. Settled life brought people into close and continuous contact with their own waste and with the animals they had domesticated, so infections that mobile groups escaped became permanent. Denser populations also meant that a crop failure could not be answered by moving on. None of this made the transition reversible. A farming population that had grown beyond what foraging could support could not return to it, and the communities that adopted agriculture displaced those that did not. The ancient shift therefore succeeded as a strategy for occupying territory while making the individuals who carried it out measurably worse off, and the two facts are not in tension once the unit of success is stated clearly.

subject: 고대 이집트의 노동 조직
title: Organizing labour in ancient Egypt
content: The monuments of ancient Egypt were long attributed to slave gangs, an image that owed more to later literature than to any evidence from the period. Excavation of the settlements that housed the builders has replaced it. These were planned villages with bakeries, breweries, and clinics, and the remains of their inhabitants show injuries consistent with heavy labour together with signs that those injuries were treated. The workers were fed, housed, and buried near the works they raised, which is not how a captive population is ordinarily handled. Administrative records recovered from such sites describe a system of rotation. Crews were drawn from villages across the country, served for a period, and returned home, with obligations recorded against each community rather than each individual. The arrangement resembled a tax paid in labour rather than in grain, and it operated during the season when the river was in flood and agricultural work was impossible. The state was therefore employing a workforce that had nothing else to do, and the villages were surrendering time that would otherwise have been idle. This reading changes what the monuments demonstrate. They record not the coercion of a subject population but the reach of an administration that could count households, schedule their service, and supply the food to sustain it far from home. The ancient achievement lay in the accounting as much as in the stone, and the papyri that record the deliveries of bread and beer are, in that sense, the more remarkable artefact.

subject: 고대 문명의 역법과 천문 관측
title: Watching the sky in ancient civilizations
content: Ancient civilizations across several regions kept careful records of the sky, and the tablets, inscriptions, and alignments they left show observation sustained over centuries. Modern readers often assume that such work was undertaken to understand the heavens, and some of it certainly was. Yet the questions that these records were built to answer were mostly practical, and reading them as early astronomy misses what their compilers were doing. Two needs dominate the surviving material. The first was agricultural, since a community that plants too early or too late loses a season, and the return of a particular star before dawn marked the moment more reliably than the weather did. The second was religious and political, because festivals had to fall on the correct day and a ruler whose calendar drifted appeared to have lost the favour that legitimated him. Predicting an eclipse mattered for the same reason: an unexpected darkening was an omen, and an expected one could be managed. The precision that resulted was considerable. Babylonian scribes recorded lunar positions for so long that they could predict eclipses without any model of what caused them, working from arithmetic patterns extracted from the record itself. That achievement is easy to underrate because it lacked the geometry that later astronomy supplied. The ancient observers were not building a picture of the cosmos; they were building a calendar that would not fail, and they succeeded at the task they had set.

subject: 지식과 정당화 — 참인 믿음으로 충분한가
title: When a true belief is not knowledge
content: For a long time philosophers analysed knowledge as belief that is both true and justified. The account has obvious appeal to anyone who reflects on it. A lucky guess is not knowledge even when it turns out true, and a well-supported belief that happens to be false is not knowledge either, so both conditions seem clearly necessary. Together they appeared to be sufficient as well, and this analysis was treated as settled philosophy for a considerable period. A short paper published in the middle of the last century unsettled it with a pair of examples. Imagine someone with excellent evidence that a colleague owns a particular car, who infers from this that somebody in the office owns one. The inference is justified and the conclusion is true, yet it is true because a different colleague owns such a car while the first has merely borrowed one. The belief is justified and true, and still calling it knowledge seems wrong, because its truth and its justification have come apart. Responses to this difficulty have taken two broad forms in later epistemology. Some philosophers add a fourth condition designed to exclude the accidental connection, requiring that the justification rest on no false step. Others abandon justification entirely and require instead that the belief be produced by a process that reliably yields truth. Neither approach has proved decisive against every case, and the persistence of the problem has led some to conclude that knowledge cannot be analysed into simpler parts at all.

subject: 자유의지와 결정론의 양립 가능성
title: Freedom in a determined world
content: If every event follows from prior conditions according to fixed laws, then our choices follow too, and it becomes hard to see how anyone could have acted otherwise. Many people conclude that determinism and free will cannot both be true, and that taking physical explanation seriously means abandoning the moral practice of holding one another responsible. The argument has real force, and it is not answered by insisting that responsibility matters to us. Compatibilists in moral philosophy reply that the argument trades on an ambiguity in the phrase could have done otherwise. On one reading it means that the past and the laws might have yielded a different outcome, which determinism denies outright. On another it means that the agent would have acted differently had she wanted to, and that reading is compatible with determinism, since it asks about the relation between her desires and her conduct rather than about the fixity of the world. Freedom, on this account, is the value of acting from reasons of her own without compulsion or ignorance. Critics answer that this relocates the problem rather than resolving it, because the desires from which an agent acts were themselves produced by conditions she never chose. Compatibilists accept the point and deny that it matters morally, holding that responsibility has always tracked how a person is connected to her action rather than how she came to be the person she is. The dispute endures because each side accuses the other of changing the subject.

subject: 고대의 노예제와 노동 형태
title: Forms of bound labour in the ancient world
content: Slavery in the ancient world is often imagined on the model of plantation systems that arose much later, with a sharp line drawn between free persons and property. The evidence from ancient civilizations describes something far more varied and considerably harder to summarize. Legal status ran along a spectrum that included debt bondage for a fixed term, service owed to a temple, hereditary obligation attached to a plot of land, and outright ownership of a person who could be sold at will. Individuals moved between these conditions across a lifetime, and a single ancient household might contain several of them at once. What the categories shared was compulsion, yet the compulsion took different forms and carried very different prospects. A debt bondsman expected release at the end of his term, and his children were usually born free; a captive taken in an ancient war might be sold abroad and never return to the region of his birth. In some ancient cities enslaved people held property, conducted business, and purchased their own freedom, while in the mines of that same society others died within a few years of arriving. The single word that covers all of this conceals more than it reveals to us. Historians accordingly attend to what a given arrangement demanded and what it permitted rather than to the label attached to it. This approach makes comparison across ancient civilizations possible without assuming that a common term names a common institution, and it prevents the modern image from being read backward into periods where the arrangements it describes had not yet appeared.

subject: 의무의 근거는 어디에 있는가
title: Where obligations come from
content: We speak easily of what a person morally ought to do, and the practice is so familiar that its foundation rarely comes into question. Yet a moral obligation binds someone whether or not she wishes to be bound, and it is not obvious what could give any requirement that kind of grip. Several answers have been proposed in ethics, and each faces a difficulty that the others were designed to avoid. One tradition grounds moral duty in consequences, holding that we ought to act so as to make things go best overall. This has the virtue of explaining why morality matters, since suffering and flourishing plainly do. It struggles, however, with cases where the best outcome requires treating a person merely as a means, and that objection is not dismissed by showing that the arithmetic came out right. A second tradition grounds obligation in the will of the agent herself, arguing that a rational being who acts on a principle she could not consistently will everyone to follow contradicts her own commitments. This explains the binding force that consequences cannot, since the requirement arises from within. Critics reply that the test is too formal to yield determinate answers, and that clever description can bring almost any principle through it. A third tradition looks to justice in the relations people already stand in, holding that duties arise from the particular claims that friends and communities have upon one another. Each account captures a truth the others miss.

subject: 향신료 무역이 바꾼 항로
title: How the spice trade redrew the sea routes
content: Spices were valuable in the ancient and medieval world out of all proportion to their bulk, and this ratio shaped the routes that carried them. A cargo worth a great deal per unit of weight can bear the cost of a long voyage, insurance against loss, and the tolls levied at every point along the way, whereas grain of the same weight cannot travel far before its price exceeds what buyers will pay. The trade therefore reached across distances that ordinary commerce never crossed, and it did so for centuries before any single power controlled the whole route. What moved with the cargo mattered as much as the cargo itself. Ships that carried pepper carried sailors who knew the timing of the monsoon, merchants who kept accounts in several scripts, and the credit arrangements that allowed a cargo to be paid for in one port and collected in another. Ports along the way grew wealthy on the traffic without producing anything that passed through them, and their prosperity depended on remaining useful to people whose business lay elsewhere. When the routes shifted, such places declined sharply, and the archaeological record registers the change within a generation. The later search for a sea passage that avoided the overland stages is usually explained by the price of pepper, and the explanation is correct as far as it goes. What it understates is how much of the existing system had to be understood before anyone could think of bypassing it.

subject: 언어와 세계의 대응
title: How words attach to the world
content: A sentence can be true or false, and this truth seems to require that its parts connect to things beyond the sentence itself. The simplest philosophical account of that connection treats a name as standing for an object, much as a label stands for the thing it is fixed to. On this picture the meaning of a word is the item it picks out, and a sentence is true when the arrangement of items matches the arrangement of words. The proposal is admirably clear, and its difficulties appear as soon as it is examined closely. Names without bearers create the first problem for this view. If the meaning of a word were its object, a name for something that does not exist would be meaningless, and sentences containing it could be neither true nor false. Yet we understand such sentences perfectly well and argue about their truth. A second difficulty concerns words that pick out the same thing under different descriptions. Two names for one planet cannot differ in meaning if meaning is the object, and yet learning that they name a single body was a genuine discovery rather than a triviality. Philosophers have responded by distinguishing what a word refers to from how it presents what it refers to, so that meaning includes a mode of presentation as well as an object. Others locate meaning in the use a word has within a practice, denying that reference is the fundamental relation at all. The argument persists because each account explains what the other leaves obscure.
